title: A1 — Spellbee Practice
description: Practice the C concepts behind the Spellbee word-mask problem, from letter sets to pointers, strings, and composition counting.
context: Assume C17, ASCII character encoding, 8-bit bytes, and a 32-bit int. Input words contain uppercase A–Z. Input conversions succeed and buffers are large enough unless a question asks about failures or overflow.

letterMask starts with int mask = 0 and sets bit word[i] - 'A' for each letter using mask | (1 << bit). Bits 0–25 represent A–Z. countBits counts the set bits by repeatedly adding (mask & 1) and shifting a non-negative mask right by one.
The examples use MAX_WORDS = 20000 and MAX_LEN = 30, with char words[MAX_WORDS][MAX_LEN] and an int masks[] array. Each stored word has at most 29 letters plus its null terminator.

A candidate (called a “panagram” in the supplied bank) has exactly seven distinct letters. Its composition count X includes every dictionary entry whose letters are a subset of those seven, including the candidate itself. Repeated letters are allowed.

questions.question: In spellbee's letterMask, how is a word represented internally?
options: As an int whose lowest 26 bits record whether each letter is present
As a linked list of chars
As a hash table of letter counts
questions.explanation: Bits 0..25 map to A..Z; a bit is 1 when that letter appears at least once. This 'letter set' idea is the heart of the whole assignment.

questions.question: Which bit position represents the letter 'C' in the mask?
questions.explanation: 'C' - 'A' = 2, so letter C uses bit index 2 (value 4).

questions.question: What integer value does letterMask("CAB") return?
Why does letterMask use OR (mask | (1<<bit)) instead of addition to set a bit?
options: OR-ing an already-set bit leaves it set, so repeated letters cannot corrupt the mask
Addition does not work on ints
questions.explanation: Setting an already-set bit with | is idempotent. Addition would carry into neighbouring bits for duplicate letters and give a wrong set.

questions.question: What does letterMask("BANANA") return?
questions.explanation: Distinct letters A,B,N set bits 0,1,13 => 1 + 2 + 8192 = 8195. Duplicate A's and N's just re-set the same bits.

questions.question: The mask produced by letterMask encodes which property of a word?
options: The SET of distinct letters it contains
questions.explanation: Two words with the same distinct letters (in any order, any counts) produce the same mask.

questions.question: Which standard header declares scanf and printf?
questions.explanation: Standard input/output functions such as scanf and printf are declared in <stdio.h>.

questions.question: Which token is the bitwise OR operator in C?
questions.explanation: A single | is bitwise OR (per-bit); || is logical OR (whole-value, short-circuiting).

questions.question: Which token is the bitwise AND operator in C?
questions.explanation: A single & is bitwise AND; && is logical AND.

questions.question: What does the expression (mask & 1) evaluate to?
options: 1 if the lowest (least-significant) bit is set, otherwise 0
questions.explanation: AND-ing with 1 masks off every bit except bit 0, isolating the lowest bit.

questions.question: In countBits, count = count + (mask & 1) adds what on each iteration?
options: The value of the current lowest bit (0 or 1)
questions.explanation: It accumulates the lowest bit, then the loop shifts mask right so the next bit becomes the lowest.

questions.question: What is the key difference between & and && in C?
options: & operates bit-by-bit on all bits; && is a logical test that yields 0/1 and short-circuits
questions.explanation: Mixing them up is a classic bug: a & b and a && b can give very different results.

questions.question: The expression (masks[j] & masks[i]) computes which letter set?
questions.explanation: Bitwise AND keeps only bits set in both operands, i.e. the shared letters. This is the basis of the subset test.

questions.question: What does the bitwise OR of two letter masks give?
options: Their union (letters appearing in either word)
questions.explanation: OR sets a bit if it is on in either operand, giving the union of the two letter sets.

questions.question: With a 32-bit int and 0 <= bit <= 25, what does (1 << bit) compute?
options: An integer with only bit number 'bit' set to 1 (i.e. 2^bit)
questions.explanation: Left-shifting the single 1-bit by 'bit' positions produces a one-hot value of 2^bit, used to target one letter.

questions.question: (1 << 3) equals which value?
questions.explanation: Shifting 1 left by 3 gives binary 1000 = 8 = 2^3.

questions.question: For a non-negative mask in countBits, what does mask = mask >> 1 do?
options: Drops the lowest bit and shifts every other bit one place right
questions.explanation: Right shift by 1 discards bit 0 and moves bit n to position n-1, letting the loop inspect each bit in turn.

questions.question: For a non-negative int mask, why does while (mask != 0) terminate when every iteration executes mask = mask >> 1?
options: Each right shift halves the non-negative value, discarding any remainder, until it reaches 0
questions.explanation: For non-negative values, right shift by one is integer division by two. A 26-bit non-negative mask reaches zero in at most 26 iterations. Do not assume this for negative signed values.

questions.question: For a NON-NEGATIVE int, mask >> 1 is equivalent to which arithmetic operation?
questions.explanation: Right shift by 1 halves a non-negative integer, discarding any remainder.

questions.question: In C17, right-shifting a NEGATIVE signed int by one bit is:
questions.explanation: C17 makes this result implementation-defined; many implementations preserve the sign. The letter masks here are non-negative because only bits 0 through 25 are used in a 32-bit int.

questions.question: On the assumed 32-bit-int system, why does setting bit 25 for 'Z' fit safely in int?
options: 2^25 is representable as a positive 32-bit int, and 25 is less than the type width
It does not fit and overflows
questions.explanation: C does not guarantee a 32-bit int. On a 16-bit-int system, 1 << 25 has undefined behavior because the shift count is at least the width of the promoted left operand. The quiz explicitly assumes 32-bit int.

questions.question: Why are the parentheses in count = count + (mask & 1) actually required, not just stylistic?
options: Because + has HIGHER precedence than &, so count + mask & 1 would wrongly parse as (count + mask) & 1
questions.explanation: Addition binds tighter than bitwise AND. Without parentheses, the expression groups as (count + mask) & 1, which can produce a different result. Precedence specifies grouping; it does not generally specify operand evaluation order.

questions.question: Why are the parentheses in (masks[j] & masks[i]) == masks[j] required?
options: Because == has HIGHER precedence than &, so without them it parses as masks[j] & (masks[i] == masks[j])
questions.explanation: Equality binds tighter than bitwise AND. Parentheses group the expression as (masks[j] & masks[i]) == masks[j], so the intersection is the left operand of the comparison.

questions.question: In masks[i] & (1 << b), what is the precedence relationship between << and &?
options: << is higher than &, so even without the parentheses the shift happens before the AND
questions.explanation: Shift operators bind tighter than bitwise AND, so the grouping would be the same here; the parentheses are kept for clarity/safety.

questions.question: Which of these binds TIGHTEST (highest precedence) in C?
questions.explanation: Postfix [] and () are among the highest-precedence operators; assignment is near the lowest.

questions.question: What is the loop condition in letterMask's for (int i = 0; word[i] != '\0'; i++)?
options: word[i] != '\0' -- stop when the string's nul terminator is reached
questions.explanation: Walking until the '\0' is the standard way to traverse a C string of unknown length.

questions.question: The counter i is declared inside the for statement: for (int i = 0; ...). What is its scope?
questions.explanation: Since C99 a variable declared in the for-init clause is visible only within that loop.

questions.question: Which loop construct is used in while (mask != 0) { count += mask & 1; mask >>= 1; }?
questions.explanation: It uses while (mask != 0) because the number of iterations depends on where the highest set bit is.

questions.question: How many times does the letter-printing loop for (int b = 0; b < 26; b++) iterate for one panagram?
questions.explanation: It always scans all 26 letter positions A..Z and prints only the ones whose bit is set.

questions.question: For n stored words, each word with seven distinct letters triggers a scan over all n words. What is the worst-case time complexity, treating word length and mask width as bounded?
options: O(n^2): each panagram re-scans all n words
questions.explanation: With up to n panagrams each scanning all n masks, Problem 3's work is quadratic in the dictionary size.

questions.question: What role does if (countBits(masks[i]) == 7) play?
options: It is a filter/selection that keeps only panagrams (exactly 7 distinct letters)
questions.explanation: Only words passing this exact-equality test produce output.

questions.question: Why does scanning b from 0 to 25 print the 7 letters already in alphabetical order?
options: Because bit 0 = A, bit 1 = B, ... so ascending bit index is ascending alphabet
It does not; order is random
questions.explanation: The mask stores letters by alphabetical bit position, so a low-to-high scan emits them sorted for free -- no sorting code needed.

questions.question: In the declaration int letterMask(const char *word), what does the leading int specify?
questions.explanation: A C function declaration reads: return-type name(parameters).

questions.question: In int letterMask(const char *word), what is 'word'?
options: A parameter: a pointer to const char
questions.explanation: word is the single formal parameter, typed as const char *.

questions.question: What restriction does const impose in the parameter const char *word?
options: The pointer variable itself can never change
The characters cannot be modified through word; the pointer variable itself can change
questions.explanation: const applies to the pointed-to char, not the pointer. Another writable alias can still modify an originally non-const object. This parameter alone does not promise that the function can never change the object by any other route.

questions.question: countBits is declared int countBits(int mask). Inside it, mask = mask >> 1 reassigns the parameter. Does that change the caller's variable?
options: Yes, it edits the caller's mask
No -- mask is a local copy passed by value, so the caller is unaffected
questions.explanation: C passes scalars by value, so countBits mutates its own copy while the caller's masks[i] stays intact.

questions.question: If main calls two helper functions, why can defining those helpers above main avoid the need for separate prototypes?
options: A function must be declared (by definition or prototype) before it is called, so defining them first lets main call them
questions.explanation: Without an earlier definition or prototype, the compiler would not know the function's signature at the call site.

questions.question: The function names letterMask and countBits follow which naming convention?
questions.explanation: camelCase starts with a lowercase word and capitalizes later words, as in letterMask and countBits.

questions.question: In scanf("%d", &total), why is &total passed rather than total?
options: scanf must receive the ADDRESS so it can store the parsed integer into total
questions.explanation: The %d conversion requires an int pointer so scanf can write into total. Passing the int value total instead is an argument-type mismatch and causes undefined behavior; it is not just an ineffective copy.

questions.question: In scanf("%s", words[i]), why is there NO & before words[i]?
options: words[i] is an array that already decays to a pointer (an address), so & is unnecessary
questions.explanation: An array name used as a value decays to the address of its first element, so words[i] is already the needed pointer.

questions.question: When letterMask(words[i]) is called, what is actually passed to the function?
options: A deep copy of all MAX_LEN chars
A copy of the POINTER to the first char (the row decays to char*)
questions.explanation: Arrays are never deep-copied as arguments in C; the function receives a pointer to the original storage.

questions.question: What is C's fundamental argument-passing model?
options: Always pass by VALUE (pointers are used to emulate pass-by-reference)
questions.explanation: Everything is copied into parameters; to let a callee modify a caller's object you pass that object's address.

questions.question: Because &total is given to scanf, scanf is able to:
options: Modify total in the caller (store the input count into it)
questions.explanation: Holding the address, scanf can write the parsed value straight into the caller's variable.

questions.question: As function parameters, char *word and char word[] are:
options: Effectively equivalent -- an array parameter is adjusted to a pointer
questions.explanation: In a parameter list, char word[] is just another spelling of char *word.

questions.question: For a char *word, the expression word[i] is exactly equivalent to:
questions.explanation: Subscripting is pointer arithmetic plus a dereference: word[i] == *(word + i).

questions.question: What is char words[MAX_WORDS][MAX_LEN]?
options: A 2-D char array: MAX_WORDS rows of MAX_LEN chars, each fitting a string of at most MAX_LEN - 1 letters
questions.explanation: Each row is a fixed-size character buffer. A valid C string needs a terminating '�', so a 30-char row can store at most 29 letters plus that terminator.

questions.question: Why is MAX_LEN defined as 30 when a word has at most 29 letters?
options: To leave room for the terminating '\0' alongside 29 letters
questions.explanation: A C string needs one extra byte for its nul terminator, so capacity must exceed the longest word by at least 1.

questions.question: After a successful scanf("%s", words[i]) with enough buffer space, the stored word is terminated by:
questions.explanation: scanf("%s") appends '\0' after the token so it is a valid C string.

questions.question: After skipping leading whitespace, what normally ends the token read by scanf("%s", ...)?
options: The next whitespace character, or end-of-file
questions.explanation: %s skips leading whitespace and reads non-whitespace characters until whitespace or end-of-file (or an input error). A successful conversion appends '�'. A field width can also limit the number of characters read.

questions.question: Given char words[MAX_WORDS][MAX_LEN], what is the type of words[i] before array-to-pointer conversion?
options: An array of MAX_LEN chars, which usually converts to a pointer to its first char
questions.explanation: The row has array type char[MAX_LEN]. Passing it as a function argument normally converts it to char*. sizeof words[i] and &words[i] are examples where that conversion does not occur.

questions.question: If total is an int and scanf("%d", &total) succeeds, what does it read?
questions.explanation: %d parses a decimal integer; &total gives scanf somewhere to put it.

questions.question: A program reads total, then runs for (int i = 0; i < total; i++) to read one word each time. What does the first input number represent?
options: The count W of words that follow
questions.explanation: total is read first, then the loop reads exactly that many words.

questions.question: In printf(" %c", 'A' + b), the %c prints:
options: The character whose code is 'A' + b
questions.explanation: 'A' + b is an int character code; %c tells printf to emit it as a single character.

questions.question: printf("%s :", words[i]) uses %s to print:
options: The nul-terminated string starting at words[i]
questions.explanation: %s walks from the given pointer printing chars until it hits '\0'.

questions.question: In printf(" ; %d\n", composable), what does the \n do?
options: Prints the two characters backslash and n
Emits a newline, ending the current output line
questions.explanation: \n is the newline escape; each panagram's result ends with it so outputs are one per line.

questions.question: The output code prints the word P using "%s :", each of seven sorted letters using " %c", then the count X using " ; %d\n". What is the line format?
options: P : C1 C2 C3 C4 C5 C6 C7 ; X
questions.explanation: The panagram, a colon, the 7 sorted letters, a semicolon, then the composable-word count X.

questions.question: In the declaration int mask = 0; inside letterMask, what is the type of mask?
questions.explanation: The declaration explicitly uses int. Under this quiz's 32-bit-int assumption, bits 0 through 25 fit without setting the sign bit.

questions.question: On a typical system with 32-bit int, how many bits are available in mask?
questions.explanation: The assumed int occupies 32 bits. A typical signed 32-bit int uses one bit for its sign; the 26 letter positions fit within its positive value range.

questions.question: On an ASCII system, what are the type and value of the ordinary C character constant 'A'?
questions.explanation: The ordinary character constant 'A' has type int in C, and its ASCII value is 65. This differs from the string literal "A", which is an array containing 'A' and a null terminator.

questions.question: With ASCII uppercase input, why does word[i] - 'A' yield an index from 0 to 25?
options: Because uppercase A..Z have consecutive ASCII codes, subtracting 'A' maps A->0 ... Z->25
questions.explanation: ASCII places uppercase A through Z in consecutive positions. C itself does not require alphabetic character codes to be consecutive, so this mapping assumes ASCII.

questions.question: With ASCII encoding, if word[i] is 'D', what is word[i] - 'A'?
questions.explanation: 'D' is 68 and 'A' is 65, so the difference is 3 -- the bit index for D.

questions.question: With ASCII encoding, which character has the code 'A' + 2?
questions.explanation: 'A' is 65, plus 2 is 67, which is 'C'. The print loop uses exactly this to turn a bit index back into a letter.

questions.question: With ASCII encoding, what input restriction keeps word[i] - 'A' within 0..25?
questions.explanation: Uppercase A through Z give indices 0 through 25. Other characters can produce invalid indices; shifting by a negative count or by a count at least the int width is undefined behavior. Input should be validated when this restriction is not guaranteed.

questions.question: What does #define MAX_WORDS 20000 create?
options: A preprocessor macro that is textually substituted before compilation
questions.explanation: In ordinary preprocessing-token use, MAX_WORDS expands to 20000. The macro is not a runtime variable, and its name is not replaced inside string literals.

questions.question: What is a benefit of #define MAX_LEN 30 over writing 30 everywhere?
options: A single edit point and a self-documenting name make the code clearer and safer to change
questions.explanation: Named constants reduce magic numbers and keep related sizes consistent.

questions.question: Macros such as MAX_WORDS are expanded by which part of the toolchain?
options: The preprocessor, before the compiler proper
questions.explanation: Preprocessing (includes, defines, conditionals) happens first, producing a translation unit for the compiler.

questions.question: When is (masks[j] & masks[i]) == masks[j] true?
options: When word j shares exactly one letter with panagram i
When EVERY letter of word j is also in panagram i (j's letters are a subset of i's)
When word j equals panagram i
When word j is longer than i
questions.explanation: AND keeps only j's bits that are also in i; if that still equals j's full mask, none of j's bits were lost, so all of j's letters are inside i.

questions.question: Testing (masks[j] & masks[i]) == masks[j] lets the composition-count loop count words that:
options: Can be spelled using ONLY the panagram's letters (a subset is allowed)
questions.explanation: This test accepts any word whose distinct letters are a subset of the candidate's letters. Repeated letters are allowed. This quiz's rule imposes no additional mandatory-letter condition.

questions.question: Under the subset-only composition rule, does a dictionary word need all seven of a candidate's letters to be counted?
options: No -- any subset of the 7 letters qualifies
Only if it has exactly 7 distinct letters
questions.explanation: A 5-distinct-letter word whose letters all lie within the panagram still counts toward X.

questions.question: If the composition loop checks every dictionary entry, including the candidate itself, is that candidate counted in its own total?
options: Yes -- its mask is a subset of itself, so (m & m) == m holds
Only when it has no repeated letters
questions.explanation: Every mask is a subset of itself, so a panagram always contributes at least 1 to its own X.

questions.question: In this study bank, what does the filter countBits(mask) == 7 require of a 'panagram'?
options: A word of at least 7 letters
A word with EXACTLY 7 distinct letters -- no more, no fewer
A word made only of vowels
questions.explanation: The exact-equality check countBits(mask) == 7 encodes 'exactly seven distinct letters'.

questions.question: Why is PERFORMANCE (9 distinct letters) rejected as a panagram?
options: countBits returns 9, and 9 != 7 fails the filter
questions.explanation: More than 7 distinct letters fails the exact == 7 test, just as fewer than 7 would.

questions.question: If a loop visits words[i] with i increasing from 0 to total - 1 and immediately prints each qualifying word, in what order are the results printed?
options: The order they appear in the input list
questions.explanation: The main loop walks words by increasing index, so output follows input order.

questions.question: To count all dictionary entries composable from a candidate's letters using the subset test, which entries must be considered?
options: Only words appearing after the panagram
questions.explanation: Every stored word is tested for the subset property, which is why the words are kept in memory.

questions.question: Inside main, char words[20000][30] is declared without static. What storage does it have?
options: 600,000 bytes of automatic storage, typically placed on the stack
questions.explanation: The array contains 20000 × 30 = 600,000 C bytes. A block-scope declaration without static has automatic storage duration. Implementations commonly use a stack, but the C standard does not require one; stack limits can matter in practice.

questions.question: A program stores words and masks in local arrays with fixed capacities supplied by #define constants. How does it avoid malloc/free for that storage?
options: It uses a global linked list
It pre-sizes fixed arrays using the #define bounds and stores everything there
questions.explanation: Fixed-capacity arrays sidestep dynamic allocation entirely, trading some memory for simplicity.

questions.question: On a system that provides strdup, what does a successful call do?
options: Allocates new memory and copies a string into it, returning a pointer the caller must later free
questions.explanation: strdup allocates space for a copy including the null terminator. Check for NULL on allocation failure and free a successful result after use. strdup is provided by POSIX but is not part of the ISO C17 library.

questions.question: If you DID use malloc/strdup to store the words, when should the memory be freed?
options: Once you are finished using the stored words, before the program exits, to avoid leaks
Inside the loop while still using it
questions.explanation: Free after last use and before exit. Freeing too early invalidates the data; never freeing leaks it.

questions.question: main is declared int and ends with return 0;. What does returning 0 signify?
options: Successful termination, communicated to the host environment
questions.explanation: Returning 0 from the initial call to main indicates successful termination. EXIT_SUCCESS also indicates success, and EXIT_FAILURE indicates failure; the meaning of other exit values depends on the implementation.

questions.question: For a nonzero unsigned mask, which operation clears its lowest set bit, allowing a population-count loop to run once per set bit?
options: mask &= (mask - 1), which clears the lowest set bit so the loop runs once per set bit
questions.explanation: mask &= (mask - 1) clears the lowest set bit. In a while (mask != 0) loop, each iteration removes one set bit. This can reduce iterations for sparse masks; it does not guarantee faster execution on every machine.

questions.question: If scanf's return value is ignored, what should a more robust program do?
options: Check it to detect malformed input or end-of-file
questions.explanation: scanf returns the number of input items assigned, or EOF if an input failure occurs before the first conversion. For these calls, require a return value of 1 before using the input. Also validate the word count and word lengths.

questions.question: With char words[20000][30], what risk exists if scanf("%s", words[i]) receives a token longer than 29 letters?
options: scanf("%s") has no width limit, so it could overflow words[i] -- a buffer overflow
questions.explanation: The unbounded %s conversion can write beyond the 30-byte row, including its null terminator. %29s bounds this write, but an overlong token leaves characters unread; robust input handling should also detect and reject such input.

questions.question: The study bank uses 'panagram' for a word with seven distinct letters. Which usual term describes text containing every letter of a specified alphabet?
questions.explanation: The usual term is pangram. This study bank retains 'panagram' from the supplied questions for the seven-distinct-letter candidates; it does not mean a palindrome or an anagram.
